messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Patel is a 36-year-old accountant who came to treatment after years of telling himself that what happened in his childhood should no longer have this much power over him. He grew up in a small apartment where nights were unpredictable because of his father’s violence toward his mother. What he remembers most clearly is not a single incident but a recurring scene: the sharp crash of metal bowls or a slammed cabinet door from the kitchen, his mother’s breathless crying, his father’s footsteps moving fast through the hallway, and the sense that the whole apartment had turned dangerous in an instant. As a boy he would freeze in his room, listening for whether the sounds were getting closer, certain that nothing he did could stop what was happening. No one outside the family intervened, and in his mind the people responsible simply went on with their lives. Even now, he says with bitterness, there were never any consequences.

He has great difficulty narrating those experiences in a coherent way. When he tries, his speech stalls and he drifts into fragments—“the dishes,” “my mother against the counter,” “his shoes in the hall”—as if the memory comes back as sensory pieces rather than a story. Remembering does not feel like looking back. It brings the same terror into his body that he felt as a child, so quickly that he often loses words and sits rigidly in the chair, jaw tight, arms braced on his knees. He describes it as being overtaken without warning, as though something in the room has opened a trapdoor beneath him.

That happens often in his daily life. Working as an accountant in a busy office, he is especially shaken by abrupt domestic-sounding noises that echo the apartment of his childhood: a coworker dropping a metal water bottle in the break room, a cabinet door banging in the office kitchen, raised voices from behind a closed conference room door. In those moments his shoulders lock, his chest tightens, and he scans before he is even fully aware of what he is looking for. He has learned to sit where he can see the doorway and the hallway beyond it. He notices exits immediately in any room and startles hard at sounds other people dismiss. What frightens him most is how instantly these cues can pull him back into the old scene, and how little control he feels over the shift.

Over time, Arjun has come to believe that bad things happen because the people who cause harm are not stopped, and that he is the kind of person to whom this can keep happening. That sense of helplessness keeps his body in a near-constant state of readiness. He says he feels tense from the moment he wakes up, as if danger could break through ordinary life at any second. The same beliefs also shape how the memories return. Because he is certain there was no accountability and no protection then, the past does not feel finished to him; it remains unresolved and current, making the old scenes easier to re-enter and harder to place at a distance.

The reverse is also true. When a memory is triggered at work or at home, the terror in it seems to confirm his bleakest conclusions. He does not come away thinking, that was only a reminder. He comes away feeling once more that he is powerless, that safety is unreliable, and that the world allows cruelty to pass unchecked. After one episode in the office kitchen, when a slammed microwave door sent a shock through him so strong that his hands trembled over a spreadsheet, he spent the rest of the day convinced he would never be a happy person again, only someone managing eruptions of dread. The more these memories break in, the more fixed that view of himself has become.

His physical alarm then feeds the cycle further. When he is already wound tight and watchful, small sounds are enough to set off full recollections; he says his body seems to remember before his mind does. And after these surges—heart pounding, muscles clenched, eyes searching—he is left feeling even more certain that he has no real protection against what might come next. The constant vigilance makes the world feel dangerous, and that atmosphere of danger makes the old violence easier to feel as if it is happening again.

By the time he sought help, Arjun was exhausted by living this way. His divorce had deepened his conviction that he had lost whatever part of him was once light or hopeful, and he was ashamed of how miserable and guarded he had become. He finally came in after realizing he was structuring his entire workday around avoiding the break room and any closed-door conversations he could hear through the wall. What he wants most is to stop feeling hijacked by noises and fragments he cannot put into words. What he fears most is that the terror means the violence never really ended inside him, and never will.
